Finding: Keep the original regional-depth equation as the benchmark, the half MLD shift as the leading onset hypothesis, and the full MLD shift as the leading profile-magnitude hypothesis. The onset tables change the earlier RMSE-only preference for the full shift. None is yet a validated universal winner.

The 21 October export contains 304 registrations: 277 complete and 27 without completed results. The complete entries comprise 255 posterior evaluations and 22 prior-predictive fits. Six posterior evaluations reuse older controls, leaving 249 distinct completed posterior fits. The original historical full-data 250 m fit is an additional, separate reference.

Of the 249 distinct completed posterior fits, 137 pass the review convergence screen and 104 also have zero tree-depth hits. The screen requires max Rhat <1.01, minimum bulk/tail ESS >=400, no sampling divergences and minimum E-BFMI >=0.3. Poor-diagnostic models are retained, but a small error does not make them ready for scientific inference.

The saved original fit used 255,369 observations at 10–250 m, four chains, 5,000 iterations with 1,000 warmup per chain, and k=15. It had max Rhat 1.001655, minimum bulk ESS 3,680, zero divergences, zero tree hits and minimum E-BFMI 0.701. It sampled well. Its in-training errors cannot be ranked against the newer held-out errors, and exact training membership was not reconstructed.

The early MLD-only depth smooth produced validation RMSE about 1.925, compared with about 1.463 for the model retaining region-specific depth smooths. Shared global depth surfaces also generally underperformed regional curves. The current evidence supports keeping distinct regional vertical structure.

Allowing residual sigma to differ by Region reduced matched additive-model validation RMSE from 1.4650 to 1.4301 and 90% interval score from 7.340 to 5.492, a 25% reduction. The first regional fit had a divergence and tree hits; later tuned regional models reproduced this performance with clean diagnostics. Region-specific residual variation is a stronger established improvement than the original additive or numeric-by MLD changes.

Regional plus depth-varying sigma improved interval scores further in the follow-up tests: interaction model 5.440 to 4.913. However, RMSE worsened from 1.4161 to 1.4442, coverage fell from 90.4% to 85.8%, and runtime rose from about 25.0 to 51.0 hours. This is a real scoring/calibration trade-off, not an automatic reason to accept or reject the model.

An additive standardized MLD effect, a numeric-by MLD smooth, and joint MLD/distance varying-coefficient smooths gave little consistent improvement over the original mean equation on the reserve set. For example, F05 interaction versus F01 original changed primary RMSE 1.4272 to 1.4169 but reserve RMSE 3.0406 to 3.0456. Those comparisons do not establish that MLD is irrelevant; they show that its mathematical representation matters.

With numeric mld_z, s(depth, by=mld_z) represents mld_z multiplied by a smooth function of depth. It permits a depth-dependent linear MLD effect. It does not provide an arbitrary nonlinear depth–MLD surface or directly estimate a vertical translation of the profile.

Topic: Full MLD shift: magnitude and shape
Finding: At 10% training, s(depth-MLD, by=Region) reduced primary/reserve RMSE from 1.4272/3.0406 to 1.4010/2.9365, with no divergences or tree hits. At 20%, it reduced 1.5398/2.7387 to 1.5053/2.6234, again with clean diagnostics. Shape RMSE and error in the MLD ±20 m neighbourhood also improved. Primary/reserve profile-RMSE bootstrap intervals still include zero in these comparisons.

Topic: Full MLD shift: onset is not clearly better
Finding: At 10% training and the 50% enhancement threshold, the full shift changed onset MAE by -0.56 m on 57 jointly detected primary casts and +0.86 m on 59 reserve casts. Both exploratory intervals include zero. At 20%, the reserve difference is +2.20 m on 56 common detections. A lower whole-profile error does not establish improved onset localization.

For depth-0.5*MLD at 10% training, onset MAE on the identical 60 primary casts is 11.17 versus 15.95 m, a 4.78 m reduction. The exploratory date-cluster bootstrap interval for the difference is [-7.56,-1.94] m. On the identical 59 reserve casts it is 14.56 versus 18.20 m, a 3.64 m reduction, interval [-6.09,-1.19] m. These are conditional expected-profile detections, not all-cast onset errors.

The 10% half-shift onset advantage also appears at 25% and 100% enhancement thresholds on primary validation; reserve support is clearer at 25%/50% than at 100%. At 20% training the 50% threshold improvement is smaller, and its intervals cross zero; that fit has one divergence. The date-blocked half shift improves matched onset MAE by 2.63 m on 86 casts and has clean diagnostics. No repeat-seed/robust-sampler half-shift fit was included in this campaign.

MAE is evaluated only when the observed curve and both compared model curves have a detected onset, using the same casts. This avoids comparing easy detections in one model with harder ones in another. False positives, false negatives, left/gap censoring and inadequate support remain visible. At 10% training, half shift has 3 reserve false positives and 5 false negatives, versus 3 and 3 for the original. Better localization does not mean every detection measure improves.

Onset is the first sustained crossing of +0.25, +0.5 or +1.0 chl_norm above the surface baseline, starting at or below 15 m. The main +0.5 threshold means 50% enhancement. Diagnostic profiles use a 1 m grid, a 5 m running median and five consecutive 1 m points, with no extrapolation beyond observed support and no interpolation across gaps >3 m. This is an operational enhancement-onset measure, distinct from the chlorophyll maximum or a universal DCM boundary.

One reserve cast, Central RS 206 on 8 October 2011, has only one saved depth at 10 m. It cannot locate an onset. The repair flags its onset as insufficient_support while retaining it in ordinary profile scores. All 34 onset cases now complete; missing support is neither a missed DCM nor evidence that no DCM exists.

Topic: Peak depth and calibration still need work
Finding: At 10% training, original/full-shift/half-shift peak-depth MAE is 18.61/21.20/21.34 m on primary and 17.32/19.67/19.66 m on reserve. Primary 90% interval coverage is 90.2%/88.3%/88.8%; reserve coverage is 88.7%/86.8%/88.3%. The original equation remains a useful control for peak location and calibration even where shifted models improve RMSE or onset.

Topic: Population predictions are a separate target
Finding: With date/ENSO effects set to zero, the 10% original/full/half validation RMSE is 1.577/1.523/1.541. However, matched half-shift onset improvement is only -0.90 m on primary and -0.73 m on reserve, with intervals crossing zero. At 20%, zero-group-effect onset errors can worsen for both shifts. The clearest onset gain therefore concerns predictions conditional on group effects; transfer to a typical or entirely new group is not established.

The depth/MLD ratio generally worsened RMSE, peak errors and sampling behaviour. The absolute-depth plus shifted-depth hybrid did not outperform the simpler anchors. Full shift with distance-dependent shape achieved the lowest eligible primary point RMSE, 1.3904, but had six divergences; its 20% version had three. These stay visible as exploratory fits rather than being selected on their lowest error alone.

The tested region-specific three-dimensional tensor fits had RMSE roughly 4.69–8.88 and none passed the convergence screen. Some region-specific depth–MLD tensors scored better than other tensor alternatives but showed substantial sensitivity and sampling problems. The current results favour modest regional smooths and targeted predictor transformations over the tested high-dimensional surfaces. This does not show that all possible tensor formulations are unsuitable.

Adding a cast random intercept did not improve held-out whole-cast RMSE in the targeted comparisons; flexible cast curves performed worse and had diagnostics problems. Fixed-nu Student-t tests worsened RMSE and had around 82% coverage. An earlier freely estimated Student likelihood improved MAE for some fits while worsening RMSE and calibration. None is a clear replacement for the current Gaussian regional-sigma baseline.

Median within-cast lag-one residual correlation is about 0.97 in leading fits. This is dependence of depth residuals, not MCMC autocorrelation. The matched constant-sigma AR1 test improved RMSE 1.4642 to 1.4430 but worsened interval score 7.346 to 7.447, and did not eliminate the profile residual pattern. AR modelling has not yet been adequately tested together with the best shifted mean equation and regional sigma.

Topic: Training size is not a monotonic result
Finding: For the original regional-sigma model, changing primary training from 10% to 20% worsened primary RMSE 1.4272 to 1.5398 but improved reserve RMSE 3.0406 to 2.7387. An alternative 10% training set also changed results substantially. Larger samples change the representation of extreme casts and dates, and the learned mean/residual scale. The evidence does not justify choosing less training data because one validation score is lower.

The registry retains three historical 5% training entries, all without completed posterior results, but no new onset/targeted/follow-up posterior fits use less than 10% training. The main 10% subset contains 108 casts and about 15,228 observations; 20% has 216 casts and 50% has 540. Primary validation has 108 casts, date-blocked validation 117, and reserve 108. Choosing entire casts prevents within-profile training/validation leakage.

For the original 10% regional-sigma model, Central RS cast 117 on 28 September 2011 accounts for 56.1% of reserve squared error, and the worst five account for 86.6%. The full shift reduces error beyond that one cast, but its reserve gain falls from 0.104 RMSE units to 0.021 after the same five reference-error casts are omitted from both models. Those omissions are influence checks only; full-data scores remain the reported result.

Overall cast-weighted RMSE weights regions according to their numbers of casts. A gain for an extreme Red Sea cast can dominate changes elsewhere. The supplied tables retain every region, depth/predictor stratum and cast; regional results and equal-region summaries should accompany any scientific selection. The data do not establish a universal MLD response across all basins.

Custom versus default original-baseline priors changed primary conditional RMSE only slightly, for example 1.4628 versus 1.4597 at 10% training. Different shrinkage choices can change stability, CPU cost and allocation between group and population effects. The custom prior predictive distributions remain broad: full-shift 5th–95th quantiles are about [-17.4,19.4]. They are scale checks rather than a guarantee of plausible profiles or an accuracy ranking.

The campaign response is enhancement, (Chl-surface_Chl)/surface_Chl, with the established surface preprocessing retained. chl_norm=0 means the surface baseline; +0.5 means 50% enhancement. Gaussian predictive draws below -1 correspond to negative chlorophyll on this scale. The leading 10% conditional fits produce about 6% of such draws, while the observed fraction is much smaller. The current likelihood does not fully respect the physical lower tail; clipping predictions would hide the problem.

k limits available smooth complexity; penalization also controls the fitted curve. The original 250 m k=15 does not establish the necessary k for a 150 m shifted coordinate. In the full-shift check, k=7 to 10 changes RMSE 1.4010 to 1.4010 on primary and 2.9365 to 2.9357 on reserve, while peak-depth error increases. k=7 is a defensible current starting point, not a proven global optimum.

Early two-chain 500-warmup/500-retained fits often had Rhat around 1.02 and low ESS, even when prediction errors were stable. A large number of observations does not guarantee that fewer MCMC iterations suffice. Four chains, 1,000 warmup and 2,000 retained draws per chain give strong diagnostics for the simpler leading models. This is a supported working configuration, not a demonstrated minimum or a guarantee for full-data fits.

0.95 is adequate for several simpler primary-split fits, but not all equations or subsets. Raising delta to 0.99 and warmup to 2,000 removes some divergence problems while leaving prediction errors almost unchanged. For the full shift, that combined change raises runtime from 4.45 to 10.15 hours. It was a two-setting change, so its effects cannot be attributed to adapt_delta alone. Resolve model-specific divergences before interpreting final parameter uncertainty.

The original warning was real: the early MLD-varying depth-10 fit hit its cap on 997 of 1,000 retained draws. Increasing the cap resolved many truncations without meaningfully changing prediction errors. Depth 12 still truncates many later regional-sigma fits; depth 14 works well for several simpler models. Tree hits are an efficiency warning separate from divergence and convergence validity warnings. More tree depth is not intrinsically a better ecological model.

Four threads per chain often reduce wall time. Controlled follow-up comparisons on the same CPU model showed roughly 1.7–2.5-fold speedups over two threads, with different core-hour trade-offs and hosts. Four chains with four threads require 16 allocated CPUs. Reused onset controls used two threads, while new onset fits used four; their raw time ratios mix model changes and CPU allocation. No universal hardware speedup is claimed.

The controlled same-cast 250 m original-equation bridge achieved 10–150 m validation RMSE 1.4408 versus 1.4628 for the corresponding 150 m fit. Fitting deeper observations can influence the shallow curve. The historical 250 m model is useful context, but this is not a comparison on identical training rows and does not overturn the newer regional-sigma/MLD tests.

Primary and reserve cohorts have repeatedly informed model development, so reserve is no longer an untouched final test. Date-blocked validation is harder and has only 13 nested date groups; bootstrap intervals are conditional on the observed regional/date structure and are exploratory, without adjustment for searching many models. A fresh cruise/date-blocked final evaluation is needed before publication-level claims about generalization.

The most useful next comparison is the half shift versus full shift versus original, with clean repeat seeds, supported regional sigma, and validation aimed at unseen dates/cruises and zero-group-effect profiles. If the half shift remains useful, compare intermediate fixed shifts or estimate a suitably constrained shift coefficient. No current result proves that 0.5 is a physical constant or the optimal coefficient.

All 1,136 aggregate RMSEs were recomputed from individual-cast errors, with maximum discrepancy 7.82e-14. All 360 onset aggregate summaries were independently checked against saved cast-level results. A further optional check of every saved model-pair record was blocked by automatic approval review after an unexpected telemetry request; it was not retried. Saved all-pair tables remain labelled as source results, not independently reverified in this review.
